idiom_name: std::variant<Cases...> + std::visit with an overload set
implementation_notes: `std::variant<Card, Transfer>` is a closure-safe tagged union: the alternative list is fixed at declaration, the active alternative is tracked, and `std::visit` applies an overload set to it - the standard makes the call ill-formed unless the visitor can be invoked for every alternative, which is C++'s compile-time totality check (cppreference documents the INVOKE requirement and `std::bad_variant_access` for the valueless state). Cases are ordinary value structs, `overloaded{...}` assembles the visitor from lambdas, and `const` on the variant supplies the immutability half. Fall back to the hand-rolled discriminated union (enum tag plus a union member in a struct) or to a class hierarchy with protected constructors and final cases when the toolchain is pre-C++17, when cases need identity or virtual dispatch, or when variants must be addable without recompiling consumers; that classic form is also what the language's own docs show before recommending `std::variant`.
pitfalls: A generic `[](auto&&)` overload in the visitor set silently absorbs every alternative, including future ones, exactly like a catch-all arm in a `switch`.

`std::variant` can become `valueless_by_exception()` if a constructor or assignment of the active alternative throws; every later `std::visit`/`std::get` then throws `std::bad_variant_access`, so throwing alternatives need a recovery path.
Alternatives must be distinct types: two structurally identical alternatives make `std::get<T>` ill-formed - wrap them in tag structs.
Immutability is per-object: a non-const variant is writable through `std::get<T>(v).field = x`, so interfaces must take `const&` (or use `std::as_const`) to keep the value closed and immutable.
